Appendix A Molecules description

A.1 H-chain

Hydrogen chains are widely used as benchmark systems because they combine strong, tunable electron correlation with a simple, scalable geometry Chan and Head-Gordon (2002); Motta et al. (2017); Motta et al. (2020), and are generally used for benchmarking quantum algorithms for state preparation. The most common form of a hydrogen chain is defined by selecting the desired number of hydrogen atoms and placing them equidistantly in a linear configuration with bond distance rr. In standard settings, the number of electrons equals the number of hydrogen atoms. In our case, we selected a chain of eight hydrogen atoms separated by a bond distance r=1.5r=1.5 Å. The initial SCF calculation was performed with the cc-pVTZ Kendall et al. (1992) basis set. To recover additional correlation, we performed an MP2 Møller and Plesset (1934) calculation on top of the SCF one. From the obtained wavefunction, we built the 1-RDM and computed the natural orbitals, restricted to the virtual space, defining a set of Frozen Natural Orbitals (FNOs). The active space is then defined by combining canonical HF orbitals for the occupied space with the leading FNOs for the virtual space. In total, the active space is composed of 8 electrons in 8 orbitals, i.e., 16 qubits. Additionally, the particle number operator was added as a penalty with a coefficient of 0.1. The reference energy, obtained with a CASCI calculation, is −9.057128-9.057128 Ha.

A.2 Complex A

Complex A used in this work is TLD-1411 (rac-[Ru(bpy)2(IP-3T)]Cl2) Monro et al. (2019), employed in place of TLD-1433 for computational practicality. TLD-1411 is a ruthenium(II) polypyridyl complex and a very close structural analogue of TLD-1433 (rac-[Ru(dmb)2(IP-3T)]Cl2), a drug currently undergoing human clinical trials for the treatment of non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer. The two compounds share an almost identical molecular scaffold and highly similar electronic structures. The only structural difference lies in the ancillary ligands: TLD-1411 contains bpy (2,2’-bipyridine) ligands, while TLD-1433 contains dmb (4,4’-dimethyl-2,2’-bipyridine) ligands.

The presence of methyl substituents in the dmb ligand introduces minor electronic and steric effects, leading to very similar absorption properties, excited-state energetics, and photochemical pathways relevant to their therapeutic activity. The qualitative trends obtained for TLD-1411 are therefore expected to be directly transferable to TLD-1433, without affecting the generality of the conclusions.

The geometry of TLD-1411 was optimized in water using the Conductor-like Polarizable Continuum Model (C-PCM) Truong and Stefanovich (1995); Barone and Cossi (1998). Calculations employed the PBE0 functional Ernzerhof and Scuseria (1999); Adamo and Barone (1999) together with the def2-TZVP basis set Weigend and Ahlrichs (2005) in the Orca code Neese (2012). The identification of the relevant occupied molecular orbitals used to construct the active spaces required for a reliable description of the excitations investigated in this work was carried out following the procedure outlined in Ref. Tarocco et al. (2025). The resulting active spaces include orbitals originating from two main regions of interest within the molecule: the ruthenium center and the elongated thiophene tail (further details can be found in Ref. Tarocco et al. (2025)). For the occupied space, we employed canonical Unrestricted Hartree-Fock orbitals obtained from a Δ\Delta-SCF Gilbert et al. (2008) calculation using the def2-SVDP Rappoport and Furche (2010) basis set in water and the cc-PVDZ-pp pseudopotential Andrae et al. (1990). The virtual space was defined using Frozen Natural Orbitals generated from an unrestricted MP2 calculation, tailored to the specific canonical occupied orbitals. In particular, we selected active space sizes composed of 14, 20, …, 50 orbitals, resulting in 28, 40, …, 100 qubits, with 14, 20, …, 50 particles.

All DMRG reference energies and approximated eigenstate estimates, reported in Tab. 3 and Tab. 4 respectively, are obtained using the Block2 Zhai et al. (2023) implementation of the algorithm. Given the unrestricted nature of the orbitals, the non-spin-adapted DMRG mode SymmetryType.SZ was used for all calculations. We stress that the reference energies are approximations of the true ground state given a specific bond dimension. The true ground state may lie slightly lower than the reported reference energies. Energies in Tab. 3 are computed using state-specific DMRG targeting the lowest singlet state, imposing spin=0.

To compute the lower bound on the overlap as described in Appendix G, we require approximations of several eigenstates of the Hamiltonians. The values reported in Tab. 4 are obtained in a mixed fashion. The two singlet roots S0 and S1 are obtained by performing a two-root state-averaged DMRG calculation followed by refinement with state-specific DMRGs using an orthogonality projector (to prevent the second root from collapsing onto S0). Two further eigenstates have been computed: the lowest triplet state T1T_{1} and the lowest quintet state QQ. For these, we run two independent state-specific DMRG calculations targeting the lowest solution with spin=2 for T1 and spin=4 for the quintet QQ.

Since Majorana monomials can break all number, zz-spin, and S2S^{2} symmetries, S1⊤S_{1}^{\top} was selected to be the smaller of the T1 and QQ state energies. Other possible candidates for S1⊤S_{1}^{\top} could include doublet states with one extra or one missing electron; however, even-length Majorana monomials from the Majoranic pool Miller et al. (2026) construct states that are superpositions of Fock states of the same parity as the Hartree-Fock state, so we omit these states from our analysis. Given that Ru(II) polypyridyl complexes are low-spin d6 closed-shell systems, their lowest excitations correspond to single-electron transitions of singlet and triplet spin multiplicities. Other multiplicities would require higher excitation manifolds and lie significantly higher in energy. We verified this computationally, confirming that no low-lying quintet or septet states are present.

Appendix B Electronic Structure Problem

In the second quantization representation, the Fock space of NN spin-orbitals (or Fermionic modes) is spanned by the set of basis states or Slater determinants, |D⟩=|n1,n2,…,nN⟩|D\rangle=|n_{1},n_{2},\dots,n_{N}\rangle, where np∈{0,1}n_{p}\in\{0,1\} denotes the occupation number of the pp-th spin-orbital. The Fermionic creation and annihilation operators that act on this space are defined as

ap†|n1,n2,…,0p,…,nN⟩=(−1)∑q=1p−1nq|n1,n2,…,1p,…,nN⟩,\displaystyle a_{p}^{\dagger}\,|n_{1},n_{2},\dots,0_{p},\dots,n_{N}\rangle=(-1)^{\sum_{q=1}^{p-1}n_{q}}\,|n_{1},n_{2},\dots,1_{p},\dots,n_{N}\rangle, (9)

and

ap|n1,n2,…,1p,…,nN⟩=(−1)∑q=1p−1nq|n1,n2,…,0p,…,nN⟩\displaystyle a_{p}\,|n_{1},n_{2},\dots,1_{p},\dots,n_{N}\rangle=(-1)^{\sum_{q=1}^{p-1}n_{q}}\,|n_{1},n_{2},\dots,0_{p},\dots,n_{N}\rangle (10)

respectively. These operators satisfy the anticommutation relations

{ap,aq}={ap†,aq†}=0,{ap,aq†}=δp​q.\{a_{p},a_{q}\}=\{a_{p}^{\dagger},a_{q}^{\dagger}\}=0,\qquad\{a_{p},a_{q}^{\dagger}\}=\delta_{pq}. (11)

The Fermionic vacuum state |vacf⟩\ket{\mathrm{vac}_f} is a unique state satisfying ap​|vacf⟩=0a_{p}\ket{\mathrm{vac}_f}=0 for all p=1,…,Np=1,\ldots,N. All other basis states, collectively forming the Fock space, are generated by applying creation operators to the vacuum:

|n1​n2​…​nN⟩:=∏p=1N(ap†)np​|vacf⟩.\ket{n_1 n_2 \ldots n_N}:=\prod_{p=1}^{N}(a_{p}^{\dagger})^{n_{p}}\ket{\mathrm{vac}_f}. (12)

The NN-mode second-quantized Fermionic Hamiltonian can be expressed in terms of creation and annihilation operators as

H=∑p,q=1Nhp​q​ap†​aq+∑p,q,r,s=1Nhp​q​r​s​ap†​aq†​ar​as,\displaystyle H=\sum_{p,q=1}^{N}h_{pq}a_{p}^{\dagger}a_{q}+\sum_{p,q,r,s=1}^{N}h_{pqrs}a_{p}^{\dagger}a_{q}^{\dagger}a_{r}a_{s}, (13)

where hp​qh_{pq} and hp​q​r​sh_{pqrs} are the one-electron and two-electron integrals, respectively.

Alternatively, the Fermionic space can be defined using Majorana operators {mk}k=12​N\{m_{k}\}_{k=1}^{2N} where

m2​p−1:=ap†+ap,m2​p:=i​(ap†−ap).m_{2p-1}:=a^{\dagger}_{p}+a_{p},\qquad m_{2p}:=\text{i}(a^{\dagger}_{p}-a_{p}). (14)

The 2​N2N operators are algebraically independent, meaning that no two distinct products of Majorana operators, when ordered by index, yield the same operator. These operators are unitary, self-adjoint, and satisfy {mp,mq}=2​δp​q\{m_{p},m_{q}\}=2\delta_{pq}. Products of Majorana operators Mν=irνmν11mν22⋯mν2​N2​NM_{\nu}=\text{i}^{r_{\nu}}m^{\nu_{1}}_{1}m^{\nu_{2}}_{2}\cdots m^{\nu_{2N}}_{2N} can be represented uniquely up to a sign by a binary vector ν=(ν1,…,ν2​N)\nu=(\nu_{1},\dots,\nu_{2N}) where νi∈{0,1}\nu_{i}\in\{0,1\}, and rν=|ν|(|ν|−1)/2r_{\nu}=|\nu|(|\nu|-1)/2, where |ν||\nu| is the Hamming weight of ν\nu, called its length. The resulting 4N4^{N} Hermitian operators {Mν}ν\{M_{\nu}\}_{\nu}, referred to as Majorana monomials, form a basis for Hermitian operators.

Using Majorana monomials, the NN-mode second-quantized Fermionic Hamiltonian can be expressed as

H=∑p,q=12​Ni​cp​q​mi​mj+∑p,q,r,s=12​Ncp​q​s​r​mp​mq​mr​ms,H=\sum_{p,q=1}^{2N}\text{i}c_{pq}m_{i}m_{j}+\sum_{p,q,r,s=1}^{2N}c_{pqsr}m_{p}m_{q}m_{r}m_{s}, (15)

for real coefficients cp​qc_{pq} and cp​q​s​rc_{pqsr}. This is a direct consequence of the relationship given in Eq. (14). The expression can be restated as

H=∑ναν​Mν,H=\sum_{\nu}\alpha_{\nu}M_{\nu}, (16)

where MνM_{\nu} are Majorana monomials of length 2 or 4.

Appendix C Majorana Propagation

Surrogate Graph

One key aspect of the operator-length truncation criterion is that it enables the construction of a so-called surrogate graph. This graph symbolically tracks the propagation of monomials through the circuit, allowing different parameters θ→\vec{\theta} to be plugged in for rapid evaluation without re-evolving the entire operator for each parameter choice. This idea has been leveraged in prior work on Pauli propagation Rudolph et al. (2023); here, we use it to substantially accelerate the optimisation of gate parameters. The surrogate graph is possible because low-length monomials dominate the contribution to the expectation value, and the truncation criterion is independent of the gate parameters. This contrasts with propagation schemes that rank terms by coefficient magnitude Ryabinkin et al. (2020); Steiger et al. (2025); Ryabinkin et al. (2025): in those cases, the surrogate graph would depend on the gate parameters and would need to be reconstructed for every parameter vector, resulting in a non-continuous landscape that complicates parameter optimization. Our method, after precompilation of the surrogate graph, allows for fast evaluation of expectation values and provides analytically provable convergence guarantees Miller et al. (2025).

Truncation criteria

A central ingredient in MP is the truncation criterion used during propagation to curb the exponential growth in the number of terms. This choice directly impacts both efficiency and accuracy. MP uses operator length as its truncation rule, defined as the number of Majorana operators appearing in a monomial: monomials whose length exceeds a chosen threshold are discarded during propagation.

The original analysis of MP Miller et al. (2025) shows that for unstructured circuits composed of random length-4 monomial generators, high-length monomials are exponentially unlikely to affect expectation values. The intuition is twofold. First, in a system with NN spin orbitals (or 2​N2N Majorana modes), there are (2​Nℓ)∼𝒪⁡(Nℓ)\binom{2N}{\ell}\sim\mathcal{O}(N^{\ell}) monomials of length ℓ\ell, which grows polynomially with NN for fixed ℓ\ell. Thus, operator length induces a natural hierarchy of polynomial subspaces whose dimension increases exponentially with ℓ\ell. Second, consider the overlap of some monomial with Fock-basis states. Only paired monomials have non-zero overlap, and for a given even length 2​ℓ2\ell, there are only (Nℓ)∼𝒪⁡(Nℓ)\binom{N}{\ell}\sim\mathcal{O}(N^{\ell}) paired monomials, a vanishing fraction of the (2​N2​ℓ)\binom{2N}{2\ell} monomials of length 2​ℓ2\ell as NN grows. Consequently, high-length monomials rarely overlap with the Fock-basis state and contribute negligibly to the expectation value.

Beyond this exponential suppression, MP also exhibits a quadratic backflow suppression from high-length to low-length monomials during propagation. Even when high-length terms are generated, their influence on the low-length subspace (which dominates the expectation value) is quadratically damped. Together, these effects justify operator length as a robust truncation criterion: discarding high-length monomials greatly reduces computational cost while maintaining a controlled approximation error. The analysis in Miller et al. (2025) provides rigorous guarantees under this scheme: the approximation error decays exponentially with the truncation threshold, and computing expectation values to a fixed error for typical circuit ensembles requires only polynomial resources. These guarantees assume unstructured circuits composed of random length-4 monomial generators and random second-quantized Hamiltonians, assumptions closely aligned with ADAPT-VQE settings.

In addition to the length-based truncation criterion, one can also consider the following alternative schemes:

  • •

    Generalised length truncation: Analogous to Pauli weight in qubit systems, where {Xi,Yi,Zi}\{X_{i},Y_{i},Z_{i}\} are anticommuting qubit-local operators each contributing one unit to the weight, we define a generalized length for Majorana monomials. On each mode jj, the Fermionic-locally acting anticommuting operators are {m2​j−1,m2​j,m2​j−1​m2​j}\{m_{2j-1},\,m_{2j},\,m_{2j-1}m_{2j}\}. The generalized length of a monomial is defined as the number of Fermionic modes it acts on, irrespective of whether the action is by a single Majorana operator or a paired operator. With this definition, the number of monomials of fixed generalized length ℓ\ell is (Nℓ)​3ℓ=𝒪⁡(Nℓ).\binom{N}{\ell}3^{\ell}=\mathcal{O}(N^{\ell}). Among these, there are (Nℓ)\binom{N}{\ell} fully paired monomials, which have standard Majorana length 2​ℓ2\ell. At a fixed cutoff ℓ\ell, the generalized scheme therefore retains all paired monomials that would only be included at cutoff 2​ℓ2\ell under the standard Majorana-length definition. Equivalently, to include the same set of paired monomials, the standard scheme must raise its cutoff from ℓ\ell to 2​ℓ2\ell, increasing the total number of retained monomials from 𝒪⁡(Nℓ)\mathcal{O}(N^{\ell}) to 𝒪⁡(N2​ℓ)\mathcal{O}(N^{2\ell}). This criterion is natural in the Heisenberg picture, where the objective is to parameterize operator growth paths from the initial observable to paired monomials that overlap with the state. Under this redefinition, the same paths are retained at fixed scaling, and the theoretical analysis of Ref. Miller et al. (2025) continues to apply.

  • •

    Coefficient-magnitude truncation: Discard monomials with |cν|<τ|c_{\nu}|<\tau for a chosen threshold τ\tau, thereby controlling graph growth during propagation and retaining only terms likely to contribute.

  • •

    Coefficient-magnitude acceptance: Retain monomials with |cν|≥τ|c_{\nu}|\geq\tau irrespective of their length, prioritising potentially impactful contributions even when they are of high length.

  • •

    Paired acceptance: Retain all paired monomials, irrespective of their length. These are precisely the monomials that contribute to expectation values in the Heisenberg picture and are therefore always retained in our Heisenberg-picture simulations, in combination with length-based truncation. Although this acceptance rule permits exponentially many terms in principle, in practice it does not lead to uncontrolled growth. When the circuit is generated by length-two and length-four Majorana monomial rotations, paired monomials above the length cutoff cannot transform into other paired monomials without passing through an intermediate high-length unpaired monomial. Since such intermediate terms are not accepted, the propagation of paired monomials remains effectively bounded.

Applying these alternative schemes yields different efficiency–accuracy trade-offs. Coefficient-magnitude truncation typically accelerates evaluation, but the induced truncation depends on the gate parameters, preventing a single surrogate graph from being reused across different θ→\vec{\theta}. Conversely, coefficient-magnitude acceptance can improve accuracy by keeping large contributions even at high length, at the cost of larger graphs. When a good prior parameter θ→0\vec{\theta}_{0} is available (e.g., from rotosolve Ostaszewski et al. (2021)), one can build a locally faithful surrogate. Fix a neighbourhood Θ={θ→:|θ→−θ→0|≤δ→}\Theta=\{\vec{\theta}:\ |\vec{\theta}-\vec{\theta}_{0}|\leq\vec{\delta}\} and construct the graph by: (i) accepting monomials that exceed the acceptance threshold somewhere in Θ\Theta, and (ii) truncating monomials that remain below the truncation threshold throughout Θ\Theta. This retains terms that may become significant under plausible parameter updates while discarding those unlikely to matter, enabling fast, reusable evaluations within Θ\Theta. In contrast to methods from the literature Ryabinkin et al. (2020); Steiger et al. (2025); Ryabinkin et al. (2025), we do not use coefficient-magnitude truncation or acceptance to control the size of the Hamiltonian. In our experiments, (generalized) length truncation is the only criterion that ensures the state remains polynomial in size.

Equivalence to Schrödinger picture simulation

While MP is naturally formulated in the Heisenberg picture, it can be shown to be equivalent to a Schrödinger picture simulation under length truncation. This equivalence is particularly useful when considering the addition of gates to an existing circuit, as in ADAPT-VQE, where one often prefers to add a gate at the end of the circuit rather than at the beginning.

To understand this equivalence, consider the evolution of the initial state ϱ\varrho through the circuit CL​(θ→)C_{L}(\vec{\theta}\,) in the Schrödinger picture. Since ϱ\varrho contains exponentially many terms, a truncation scheme is again required to control growth. We begin by truncating the initial state ϱ\varrho to include only paired monomials up to length 2​ℓ2\ell. We then propagate each monomial in ϱ\varrho through the circuit CL​(θ→)C_{L}(\vec{\theta}\,) using the same branching rules as in Equation (4), but with a negative sign in front of the sin⁡θj\sin\theta_{j} term due to the reversed direction of propagation. At each step, monomials whose length exceeds 2​ℓ2\ell are discarded. After propagating through all gates, we compute the expectation value by evaluating the overlap with the observable HH.

The equivalence between the Schrödinger and Heisenberg pictures under length truncation arises because both approaches effectively track the same computational paths. In the Heisenberg picture, we track paths from the observable to the state; in the Schrödinger picture, we track paths from the initial state to the observable. In both cases, the length-based truncation criterion ensures that only paths involving low-length monomials are retained. Since only paired monomials of length up to 2​ℓ2\ell contribute to the final expectation value, both pictures consider the same set of computational paths, and consequently yield identical expectation values for any choice of parameters θ→\vec{\theta}. When coefficient-based truncation schemes are employed, however, this equivalence no longer holds, as the sets of retained paths differ between the two pictures depending on the parameter values.

Analytical gradient with respect to circuit parameters

Variational quantum algorithms rely on classical optimizers to determine optimal circuit parameters. For VQEs, gradient-based methods such as the Broyden-Fletcher-Goldfarb-Shanno (BFGS) algorithm are commonly employed. These optimisation methods require computation of the gradient, which can be approximated using finite differences or computed exactly using parameter-shift methods for certain gate types Mitarai et al. (2018). Thanks to the surrogate graph, our approach enables analytical computation of the surrogate model’s gradient.

To compute the approximate energy gradient, we express the gradient element with respect to a single parameter θj\theta_{j} of the jj-th gate as

∂∂θj​f~​(θ→)=Tr⁡[ϱj−1​∂∂θj​(Uj†​Hj+1​Uj)],\frac{\partial}{\partial{\theta_{j}}}\tilde{f}(\vec{\theta})=\Tr[\varrho_{j-1}\,\frac{\partial}{\partial{\theta_{j}}}\left(U_{j}^{\dagger}H_{j+1}\,U_{j}\right)], (17)

where Hj+1H_{j+1} is the observable back-propagated through gates (j+1)(j+1) to LL, and ϱj−1\varrho_{j-1} is the state forward-propagated through gates 11 to (j−1)(j-1). At the level of individual Majorana monomials, taking the parameter derivative yields the following branching rule for propagation through a single gate:

∂∂θj​Uj†​Mν​Uj→{0if ​[Mν,Mγj]=0,−sin⁡(θj)​Mν+i​cos⁡(θj)​Mγj​Mνif ​{Mν,Mγj}=0,−sin⁡(θj)​Mνif ​{Mν,Mγj}=0​ and truncated.\frac{\partial}{\partial{\theta_{j}}}U_{j}^{\dagger}M_{\nu}\,U_{j}\rightarrow\begin{cases}0&\text{if }[M_{\nu},M_{\gamma_{j}}]=0,\\ -\sin(\theta_j)\,M_{\nu}+\mathrm{i}\,\cos(\theta_j)\,M_{\gamma_{j}}M_{\nu}&\text{if }\{M_{\nu},M_{\gamma_{j}}\}=0,\\ -\sin(\theta_j)\,M_{\nu}&\text{if }\{M_{\nu},M_{\gamma_{j}}\}=0\text{ and truncated}.\end{cases} (18)

We implement this using a sliding-window scheme that maintains copies of both the evolved state and the Hamiltonian. The state is propagated forward up to gate j−1j-1, while the observable is back-propagated from gate j+1j+1 to gate LL. The derivative with respect to the gate parameter is then evaluated using the expression above. When multiple gates share the same parameter, the chain rule applies and we sum the individual contributions to obtain the total gradient.

This approach allows analytical computation of the surrogate model’s gradient in time proportional to a single energy evaluation. Table 5 reports the time spent on surrogate-graph preparation (preprocessing), energy evaluation, and joint energy-and-gradient evaluation. Preparing the surrogate graph is the dominant cost but is performed only once per parameter-optimization step. In contrast, energy and gradient evaluations are substantially faster, and computing the gradient in addition to the energy incurs at most a threefold overhead relative to energy evaluation alone, independent of system size and the number of ADAPT-VMPE iterations.

Efficient gradient selection for ADAPT-VQE

The ADAPT-VQE algorithm iteratively constructs a parameterized quantum circuit by selecting gates from an operator pool that best improve the variational energy. At iteration LL, the algorithm selects the unitary

UL=e−iθLMγL/2,U_{L}=e^{-i\theta_{L}M_{\gamma_{L}}/2},

which maximizes the magnitude of the energy gradient with respect to θL\theta_{L} evaluated at θL=0\theta_{L}=0.

In the Heisenberg picture, the selection gradient is given by

∂∂θL​Tr⁡[UL​ϱ​UL†​HL−1]|θL=0=−Tr⁡[HL−1​[MγL,ϱ]],\left.\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta_{L}}\Tr\!\left[U_{L}\,\varrho\,U_{L}^{\dagger}H_{L-1}\right]\right|_{\theta_{L}=0}=-\Tr\!\left[H_{L-1}\,[M_{\gamma_{L}},\varrho]\right], (19)

while in the Schrödinger picture it can be written as

∂∂θL​Tr⁡[ϱL−1​UL†​H​UL]|θL=0=Tr⁡[ϱL−1​[MγL,H]].\left.\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta_{L}}\Tr\!\left[\varrho_{L-1}\,U_{L}^{\dagger}HU_{L}\right]\right|_{\theta_{L}=0}=\Tr\!\left[\varrho_{L-1}\,[M_{\gamma_{L}},H]\right]. (20)

In these expressions, the newly selected gate is applied to the initial state or Hamiltonian, respectively.

To evaluate the commutator [MγL,ϱ][M_{\gamma_{L}},\varrho] in the Heisenberg picture, it is sufficient to retain only those terms that contribute to the trace. Assuming that only length-two and length-four Majorana operators are in the pool, and noting that a length-four Majorana generator can increase or decrease the length of a Majorana monomial in the state by at most two, capturing all terms that may appear in the evolved Hamiltonian requires setting the maximum monomial length in the initial state to ℓ+2\ell+2, where ℓ\ell is the cutoff used for the Hamiltonian. The number of terms required in the initial state, therefore, needs to be 𝒪⁡(N(ℓ+2)/2)\mathcal{O}\!\left(N^{(\ell+2)/2}\right) to include all monomials relevant to the gradient computation.

One can then compute the commutator [MγL,ϱ][M_{\gamma_{L}},\varrho] for each gate in the pool and search for it in the evolved Hamiltonian representation with 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1) complexity, since the evolved operator is stored as a hash map. Thus, for cutoff-66, the complexity is 𝒪⁡(K​N4)\mathcal{O}(KN^{4}), where KK is the number of elements in the pool.

In the Schrödinger case, we consider the commutators [MγL,H][M_{\gamma_{L}},H]. In general, there are 𝒪⁡(N4)\order{N^4} terms in second quantized Hamiltonians, so computing the commutator for each gate has complexity 𝒪⁡(K​N4)\mathcal{O}(KN^{4}) for KK pool elements, which is independent of the cutoff.

Appendix D Performance Improvements to ADAPT-VMPE

Gate selection is a vital and time-consuming part of ADAPT-VMPE. This follows from the fact that a potentially large description of the evolved Hamiltonian (up to 𝒪⁡(Ncutoff)\order{N^{\rm cutoff}} terms) must be evaluated against Θ⁡(N4)\Theta(N^{4}) pool candidates. While polynomial in principle, the time required for pool evaluation grows rapidly with the number of qubits. Below we present several non-exclusive methods by which this process can be substantially accelerated with negligible impact on circuit quality.

D.1 Pool reduction for Majoranic pool for Heisenberg ADAPT-VMPE

Suppose MνM_{\nu} and Mν′M_{\nu^{\prime}} are even-length Majorana monomials acting on the same set of modes, with the same parity of odd indices, at each mode acting with only one Majorana operator. Then there exists an even-size set JJ such that

Mν′=η​Mν​Q,Q:=∏j∈Jm¯j,η∈{±1},M_{\nu^{\prime}}=\eta\,M_{\nu}Q,\qquad Q:=\prod_{j\in J}\bar{m}_{j},\qquad\eta\in\{\pm 1\}, (21)

where each m¯j=−i​m2​j−1​m2​j\bar{m}_{j}=-im_{2j-1}m_{2j} is a paired Majorana operator. Because |J||J| is even, Q2=IQ^{2}=I. Also, QQ is diagonal in the Fock basis, so for any Fock state |n→⟩\ket{\vec n},

Q​|n→⟩=sJ​|n→⟩,sJ∈{±1}.Q\ket{\vec n}=s_{J}\ket{\vec n},\qquad s_{J}\in\{\pm 1\}. (22)

Using ei​θ​A=cos⁡(θ)​I+i​sin⁡(θ)​Ae^{i\theta A}=\cos(\theta)I+i\sin(\theta)A for involutory Hermitian AA,

ei​θ​Mν′​|n→⟩=(cos⁡θ+i​sin⁡θ​η​Mν​Q)​|n→⟩=(cos⁡θ+i​η​sJ​sin​θ​Mν)​|n→⟩=(cos⁡θ+i​sin⁡(η​sJ​θ)​Mν)​|n→⟩=(cos⁡θ+i​sin⁡(±θ)​Mν)​|n→⟩=(cos⁡(±θ)+i​sin⁡(±θ)​Mν)​|n→⟩=ei±θ​Mν​|n→⟩,\begin{split}e^{i\theta M_{\nu^{\prime}}}\ket{\vec n}&=\left(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta\,\eta M_{\nu}Q\right)\ket{\vec n}=\left(\cos\theta+i\eta s_{J}\sin\theta\,M_{\nu}\right)\ket{\vec n}\\ &=\left(\cos\theta+i\sin(\eta s_J\theta)\,M_{\nu}\right)\ket{\vec n}=\left(\cos\theta+i\sin(\pm\theta)\,M_{\nu}\right)\ket{\vec n}\\ &=\left(\cos(\pm\theta)+i\sin(\pm\theta)\,M_{\nu}\right)\ket{\vec n}=e^{i\pm\theta M_{\nu}}\ket{\vec n},\end{split} (23)

which shows that the effect of Mν′M_{\nu^{\prime}} and MνM_{\nu} on a Fock state is the same up to the change of the phase of θ\theta. This is the same orbit-equivalence mechanism observed in the Jordan-Wigner mapping in qubit space Ryabinkin et al. (2020).

D.2 Pool trimming

In the ADAPT-VMPE procedure, all gates in the predefined pool PP must be evaluated at each step to select the gate to be added to the ansatz. However, the size of typical pools consisting of single and double excitations grows as 𝒪⁡(N4)\order{N^4} with the number of qubits NN, making the pool evaluation step time-consuming for large systems. One possible solution is to evaluate only a subset Pi⊆PP_{i}\subseteq P of the pool at each step ii. To our knowledge, few studies address this problem, except Zhang et al. (2021), which uses mutual information from classical methods like DMRG to reduce the pool, and the recent work LaRose et al. (2026), in which the best pool elements are retained and supplemented with random operators each iteration.

Fixed pool trimming relies on the observation that pool elements that fail to improve the current energy at a given point are unlikely to improve it in later iterations either. This allows some elements to be removed from the pool, reducing the number of candidates to inspect. This observation is illustrated in Fig. 6, which analyzes how the selected pool elements at each iteration performed across subsequent iterations. The ranks determined from the first iteration show that the same ansatz would have been obtained using only the best 8,000 elements. In a more extreme case, keeping only the best 250 pool elements for the first 20 iterations yields the same ansatz. As the number of iterations increases, the ranks of the selected elements (as determined from the first iteration) grow; recomputing ranks at iteration 26 again yields smaller ranks for a certain number of subsequent iterations, with the same pattern repeating at iterations 51 and 76.

To implement the pool trimming procedure, we start with P1=PP_{1}=P. Each pool element pj∈Pp_{j}\in P is assigned a rank rj1∈{1,…,|P|}r^{1}_{j}\in\{1,\dots,|P|\} based on the evaluation results. Pool elements whose ranks exceed a threshold τ\tau are removed, giving P~={pj|p∈P​ and ​rj1<τ}\tilde{P}=\{p_{j}~|~p\in P\mbox{ and }r^{1}_{j}<\tau\}. For a predetermined number of steps k=2,3,…,κ−1k=2,3,\dots,\kappa-1, ADAPT-VMPE uses the trimmed pool Pk=P~P_{k}=\tilde{P}, after which the full pool is re-evaluated by setting Pκ=PP_{\kappa}=P, yielding a new set of ranks {rjκ}\{r^{\kappa}_{j}\}. This full re-evaluation is motivated by Fig. 6, which shows that as the iteration number grows, the ranks of selected elements also increase, indicating the need for periodic re-ranking.

There are two hyperparameters: pool cutoff threshold τ\tau (the number of pool elements to retain) and κ\kappa (the frequency of full pool re-evaluation). For example, for the 40-qubit Complex A case, setting τ=300\tau=300 and κ=25\kappa=25 yields the same ansatz after 100 iterations while providing a significant reduction in the number of gate evaluations.

D.3 Mixed selection procedure

Two methods dominate the literature for gate selection. The first, gradient selection, prefers gates U⁡(θ)U(\theta) that maximize the magnitude of the derivative of Tr⁡(ϱ​U†​(θ)​H​U​(θ))\Tr(\varrho U^\dagger(\theta)H U(\theta)) at θ=0\theta=0: the larger this value, the greater the expected improvement when the corresponding gate is added. The second, GGF selection Feniou et al. (2025), directly estimates the expected energy improvement when optimizing minθ⁡Tr⁡(ϱ​U†​(θ)​H​U​(θ))\min_{\theta}\Tr(\varrho U^\dagger(\theta)H U(\theta)). Depending on the generator GG, finding the optimal θ\theta may require evaluating the expectation value at only a few values of θ\theta. In particular, if GG is a Pauli string or Majorana monomial, evaluations at only 3 values are needed. A particular benefit of this method is that it not only selects a gate to be appended to the ansatz, but also proposes a good initial value for parameter optimization.

While both methods can improve the current quantum state, we found that GGF selection outperforms gradient selection, as shown in Fig. 7. On the other hand, our implementation allows much faster gradient evaluation than GGF selection. This motivates using gradient selection for pool trimming (as a fast approximate assessment) and GGF selection for the intermediate gate selection steps from the trimmed pool. As shown in Fig. 7, this mixed approach matches GGF selection in quality while being substantially faster.

Appendix E Transpilation cost analysis

E.1 All-to-all connectivity

For all-to-all connectivity, implementing Pauli exponentiation exp⁡(i​θ​P)\exp(\mathrm i \theta P) for a kk-local operator requires 2​k−2=𝒪⁡(k)2k-2=\order{k} CNOT operators, which is optimal. Both iQCC and vDBF, due to pool synthesis, can in principle select an arbitrary operator, which is why their CNOT cost may reach 𝒪⁡(N)\order{N} in the worst case. In practice, however, both algorithms are expected to select much cheaper operators. iQCC typically selects operators that are at most 4-local; these reflect Fermionic double excitation operators up to the missing ZZ Pauli strings removed by the authors, as confirmed by the log files in [29] for N2, giving 𝒪⁡(1)\order{1} cost per gate added. For similar reasons, vDBF is expected to typically select 4-length Majorana monomials. With the ternary-tree F2Q mapping Jiang et al. (2020), each Majorana operator becomes 𝒪⁡(log⁡N)\order{\log N}-local, so the product of 4 such operators is also 𝒪⁡(log⁡N)\order{\log N}-local, giving a typical CNOT cost of 𝒪⁡(log⁡N)\order{\log N} for vDBF.

SWCS, when using Fermionic-spin pool, can attain benefits from proper Fermionic-spin selection, yielding a guaranteed 𝒪⁡(log⁡N)\order{\log N} CNOT cost per gate. Otherwise, when using CEO pool, a 𝒪⁡(1)\order{1} CNOT cost per gates is achieved.

ADAPT-VMPE uses only 2- and 4-length Majorana monomials by construction. As for vDBF, the typical and worst-case CNOT cost is 𝒪⁡(log⁡N)\order{\log N}.

E.2 Heavy-hexagonal connectivity

For limited connectivity, implementing exp⁡(i​θ​P)\exp(\mathrm i \theta P) requires 𝒪⁡(kST)\order{k_{\rm ST}} CNOTs, where kSTk_{\rm ST} is the number of nodes in the Steiner tree spanned by the qubits on which PP acts. This complexity can be achieved either via the Steiner tree implementation of Miller et al. (2026) or via an appropriate SWAP sequence. The value kSTk_{\rm ST} may be as small as kk, but can also be much larger; one can formally show that kST=𝒪⁡(d​k)k_{\rm ST}=\order{dk} where dd is the maximum inter-node distance in the connectivity graph, which is 𝒪⁡(N)\order{\sqrt N} for heavy-hexagonal or 2D grid topologies. This follows by noting that a valid Steiner tree11 1 We use ‘Steiner tree’ to mean any tree connecting all the terminals, not necessarily the optimal one. can be constructed by successively connecting vertices via shortest paths and removing any resulting cycles. For randomly selected qubits, as is typical in ADAPT-VQE-like ansatz construction, this scaling is expected to hold.

From these results, iQCC requires 𝒪⁡(N)\order{\sqrt N} CNOTs in the typical scenario (and 𝒪⁡(N)\order{N} in the worst case), using the arguments from the previous subsection. Similarly, each gate added by SWCS requires 𝒪⁡(N)\order{\sqrt N} CNOTs when CEO pool is used.

For vDBF, ADAPT-VMPE and SWCS using Fermionic-spin pool, using the optimal ternary-tree mapping produces 𝒪⁡(log⁡N)\order{\log N}-local Pauli operators, requiring 𝒪⁡(N​log⁡N)\order{\sqrt{N}\log N} CNOTs. However, using a Bonsai F2Q mapping, it can be formally shown that only 𝒪⁡(N)\order{\sqrt N} CNOTs are required Miller et al. (2023), and the optimal Steiner tree for such mappings can be found in polynomial time Miller et al. (2026).

E.3 Number of RZ gates

Since iQCC, vDBF, and ADAPT-VMPE each add a single-Pauli-exponentiation operator per iteration, the number of RZ gates per gate added equals 1. For SWCS, either the Fermionic-spin pool is used Mullinax and Tubman (2025), which requires 8 RZ gates per operator upon decomposition, or the CEO pool Ramôa et al. (2025), which requires 4.

Appendix F Compilation methods for large scale benchmarks

F.1 NISQ

For all-to-all connectivity, we used the standard treespilation algorithm with Pauli string cost as described in Miller et al. (2026). We ran simulated annealing with a geometric schedule T⋅0.9995tT\cdot 0.9995^{t}, starting from 50 and ending at 1. Once the F2Q mapping is selected, we transform the Fermionic circuit into a qubit circuit, transpile using the Steiner method from Miller et al. (2026), and further fine-tune with the Qiskit transpiler at optimization level 2, with basis gates cx and u. Active rotations were not transpiled, as they are applied to the Hamiltonian.

For heavy-hexagonal connectivity, we used the topology of the IBM Fez quantum computer and ran treespilation to find a Bonsai F2Q mapping whose ternary tree preserves the topology. This also provides an initial layout used for the Steiner method. We then applied Qiskit transpilation with the IBM Fez topology using the same settings as for all-to-all connectivity.

F.2 Fault-tolerant

For FT algorithms like QPE, the cost also depends on the number of Paulis in the operator and the L1L_{1} norm of the operator coefficients. Since active rotations may increase this number, it might in general be preferable to implement them as part of the state preparation circuit. However, for the molecules considered in this paper, this does not appear to be the case, as presented in Fig. 8: operators dressed with active rotations appear to be simpler than the originals. Therefore, in the main text we present the T count for the case where active rotations are dressed to the Hamiltonian, while Fig. 9 presents both variants.

Since limited connectivity and the choice of Bonsai F2Q mapping have no impact on the number of T gates (as SWAP operators are Clifford), we selected Jordan-Wigner mapping and all-to-all connectivity. We then transpiled the qubit circuit into Clifford and ZZ-rotation gates using Steiner decomposition Miller et al. (2026), and compiled further to obtain a circuit reproducing the original state with error at most ε=10−4\varepsilon=10^{-4}. Each ZZ-rotation was decomposed into single-qubit Clifford and T gates with infidelity ε#​RZ\frac{\varepsilon}{\#\mathrm{RZ}}, using pygridsynth [30], an implementation of a variant of the Ross-Selinger algorithm Ross and Selinger (2016). After this step, the circuit consists only of Clifford and T gates, and we computed the count of the latter.

Appendix G Overlap bounds

This section is dedicated to the formal derivation of the overlap of a quantum state |ψ⟩\ket{\psi} with the ground state of a molecular Hamiltonian HH.

Theorem 1.

Let HH be a molecular Hamiltonian and let |E0⟩,|E1⟩\ket{E_0},\ket{E_1} be the ground state and first excited state with corresponding energies E0,E1E_{0},E_{1}. Let E0<E1E_{0}<E_{1}. Let |ψ⟩\ket{\psi} be a quantum state such that E≔⟨ψ|​H​|ψ⟩∈(E0,E1)E\coloneqq\bra{\psi}H\ket{\psi}\in(E_{0},E_{1}). Then

|⟨ψ|E0⟩|2≥1−E−E0E1−E0.|\innerproduct{\psi}{E_0}|^{2}\geq 1-\frac{E-E_{0}}{E_{1}-E_{0}}. (24)
Proof.

Let |ψ⟩\ket{\psi} be of the form |ψ⟩=∑iαi​|Ei⟩\ket{\psi}=\sum_{i}\alpha_{i}\ket{E_i}, where |Ei⟩\ket{E_i} are eigenvectors of HH. One has

E−E0=⟨ψ|​H​|ψ⟩−E0=∑k,mαk∗​αm​Em​⟨Ek|​|Em⟩−E0=∑k|αk|2​Ek−E0≥(1−|α0|2)​E1+|α0|2​E0−E0=(E1−E0)​(1−|α0|2),\begin{split}E-E_{0}&=\bra{\psi}H\ket{\psi}-E_{0}=\sum_{k,m}\alpha_{k}^{\ast}\alpha_{m}E_{m}\bra{E_k}\ket{E_m}-E_{0}=\sum_{k}|\alpha_{k}|^{2}E_{k}-E_{0}\\ &\geq(1-|\alpha_{0}|^{2})E_{1}+|\alpha_{0}|^{2}E_{0}-E_{0}=(E_{1}-E_{0})(1-|\alpha_{0}|^{2}),\end{split} (25)

and from this

1−|α0|2≤E−E0E1−E0,1-|\alpha_{0}|^{2}\leq\frac{E-E_{0}}{E_{1}-E_{0}}, (26)

which after basic transformation and given |α0|=|⟨ψ|E0⟩||\alpha_{0}|=|\innerproduct{\psi}{E_0}| proves the statement. ∎

The above theorem is useful when the only information about the state |ψ⟩\ket{\psi} is its energy. It effectively reflects the intuition that the worst-case overlap occurs when |ψ⟩\ket{\psi} is a superposition of |E0⟩\ket{E_0} and |E1⟩\ket{E_1}. However, solutions to molecular Hamiltonians typically belong to a subspace defined by symmetry constraints on the number, zz-spin, and S2S^{2} operators. We assume hereafter that the ground state is a singlet from a particular particle sector; the theorems can be readily adapted to other cases. We will refer to a state as non-singlet if its spin multiplicity differs from singlet or if it belongs to the wrong particle-number sector.

Theorem 2.

Let HH be a Hamiltonian and let |E0⟩,|S1⊤⟩,|S1⟩\ket{E_0},\ket{S^\top_1},\ket{S_1} be the ground state (a singlet state), the lowest-energy non-singlet eigenstate, and the first singlet excited state, with corresponding energies E0,S1⊤,S1E_{0},S^{\top}_{1},S_{1}. Let E0<S1E_{0}<S_{1}. Let |ψ⟩\ket{\psi} be a quantum state with expectation value E∈(E0,S1)E\in(E_{0},S_{1}). Let ΠS\Pi_{S} be the projection onto the space of singlet states and let |αS⊤|2=1−⟨ψ|​ΠS​|ψ⟩|\alpha_{S^{\top}}|^{2}=1-\bra{\psi}\Pi_{S}\ket{\psi} be the overlap of the state with the non-singlet space. Then

|⟨ψ|E0⟩|2≥S1−ES1−E0−|αS⊤|2​S1−S1⊤S1−E0.|\innerproduct{\psi}{E_0}|^{2}\geq\frac{S_{1}-E}{S_{1}-E_{0}}-|\alpha_{S^{\top}}|^{2}\frac{S_{1}-S^{\top}_{1}}{S_{1}-E_{0}}. (27)
Proof.

Any quantum state can be written uniquely (up to a phase of the α\alpha’s) in the following form

|ψ⟩=α0​|E0⟩+αS​|ψS⟩+αS⊤​|ψS⊤⟩,\ket{\psi}=\alpha_{0}\ket{E_0}+\alpha_{S}\ket{\psi_S}+\alpha_{S^{\top}}\ket{\psi_{S^\top}}, (28)

where |ψS⟩\ket{\psi_S} is a state orthogonal to |E0⟩\ket{E_0} satisfying ⟨ψS|​ΠS​|ψS⟩=1\bra{\psi_S}\Pi_{S}\ket{\psi_S}=1, and |ψS⊤⟩\ket{\psi_{S^\top}} is the remaining part satisfying ⟨ψS⊤|​ΠS​|ψS⊤⟩=0\bra{\psi_{S^\top}}\Pi_{S}\ket{\psi_{S^\top}}=0. Assuming all states on the right-hand side are normalized,

|α0|2+|αS|2+|αS⊤|2=1.|\alpha_{0}|^{2}+|\alpha_{S}|^{2}+|\alpha_{S^{\top}}|^{2}=1. (29)

In addition,

E=⟨ψ|​H​|ψ⟩=(α0∗​⟨E0|+αS∗​⟨ψS|+αS⊤∗​⟨ψS⊤|)​H​(α0​|E0⟩+αS​|ψS⟩+αS⊤​|ψS⊤⟩)≥|α0|2​E0+|αS|2​S1+|αS⊤|2​S1⊤+2Re(α0∗αS⟨E0|H|ψS⟩)+2Re(α0∗αS⊤⟨E0|H|ψS⊤⟩)+2Re(αS∗αS⊤⟨ψS|H|ψS⊤⟩)\begin{split}E&=\bra{\psi}H\ket{\psi}\\ &=(\alpha_{0}^{\ast}\bra{E_0}+\alpha_{S}^{\ast}\bra{\psi_S}+\alpha_{S^{\top}}^{\ast}\bra{\psi_{S^\top}})H(\alpha_{0}\ket{E_0}+\alpha_{S}\ket{\psi_S}+\alpha_{S^{\top}}\ket{\psi_{S^\top}})\\ &\geq|\alpha_{0}|^{2}E_{0}+|\alpha_{S}|^{2}S_{1}+|\alpha_{S^{\top}}|^{2}S_{1}^{\top}\\ &\phantom{=\ }+2\real(\alpha_{0}^{\ast}\alpha_{S}\bra{E_0}H\ket{\psi_{S}})\\ &\phantom{=\ }+2\real(\alpha_{0}^{\ast}\alpha_{S^{\top}}\bra{E_0}H\ket{\psi_{S^\top}})\\ &\phantom{=\ }+2\real(\alpha_{S}^{\ast}\alpha_{S^{\top}}\bra{\psi_S}H\ket{\psi_{S^\top}})\end{split} (30)

where we used ⟨E0|​H​|E0⟩=E0\bra{E_0}H\ket{E_0}=E_{0}, ⟨ψS|​H​|ψS⟩≥S1\bra{\psi_S}H\ket{\psi_S}\geq S_{1}, ⟨ψS⊤|​H​|ψS⊤⟩≥S1⊤\bra{\psi_{S^\top}}H\ket{\psi_{S^\top}}\geq S^{\top}_{1}. The last three terms all vanish. Indeed,

⟨E0|​H​|ψS⟩=E0​⟨E0|​|ψS⟩=0\bra{E_0}H\ket{\psi_{S}}=E_{0}\bra{E_0}\ket{\psi_{S}}=0 (31)

by definition of |ψS⟩\ket{\psi_S}; similarly ⟨E0|​H​|ψS⊤⟩=0\bra{E_0}H\ket{\psi_{S^\top}}=0. Finally, ⟨ψS|​H​|ψS⊤⟩=0\bra{\psi_S}H\ket{\psi_{S^\top}}=0 because [H,ΠS]=0[H,\Pi_{S}]=0 (since HH is a molecular Hamiltonian), meaning singlet states are mapped to singlet states, and the singlet and non-singlet subspaces are orthogonal. This yields

E≥|α0|2​E0+|αS|2​S1+|αS⊤|2​S1⊤=|α0|2​E0+(1−|α0|2−|αS⊤|2)​S1+|αS⊤|2​S1⊤=S1+|α0|2​(E0−S1)+|αS⊤|2​(S1⊤−S1),\begin{split}E&\geq|\alpha_{0}|^{2}E_{0}+|\alpha_{S}|^{2}S_{1}+|\alpha_{S^{\top}}|^{2}S^{\top}_{1}\\ &=|\alpha_{0}|^{2}E_{0}+(1-|\alpha_{0}|^{2}-|\alpha_{S^{\top}}|^{2})S_{1}+|\alpha_{S^{\top}}|^{2}S^{\top}_{1}\\ &=S_{1}+|\alpha_{0}|^{2}(E_{0}-S_{1})+|\alpha_{S^{\top}}|^{2}(S^{\top}_{1}-S_{1}),\end{split} (32)

where we used Eq. (29) to eliminate |αS|2|\alpha_{S}|^{2}. A simple algebraic rearrangement gives the required statement, noting that E0<S1E_{0}<S_{1} by assumption. ∎

Theorem 2 provides a bound for both S1⊤<S1S^{\top}_{1}<S_{1} and S1⊤>S1S^{\top}_{1}>S_{1}, improving upon Theorem 1 in both cases. Indeed, if S1<S1⊤S_{1}<S^{\top}_{1}, then E1≡S1E_{1}\equiv S_{1}, making the first term of the bound equal to that of Theorem 1. The subtracted term then becomes negative, contributing positively to the bound for any |α||\alpha|. If S1⊤<S1S^{\top}_{1}<S_{1}, assuming E∈(E0,S1⊤)E\in(E_{0},S^{\top}_{1}) (the range required for Theorem 1 with E1≡S1⊤E_{1}\equiv S^{\top}_{1}), the difference between the two bounds is

S1−ES1−E0−|αS⊤|2​S1−S1⊤S1−E0−S1⊤−ES1⊤−E0=(S1−E)​(S1⊤−E0)−|αS⊤|2​(S1−S1⊤)​(S1⊤−E0)−(S1⊤−E)​(S1−E0)(S1−E0)​(S1⊤−E0)=−S1​E0−E​S1⊤+S1⊤​E0+S1​E−|αS⊤|2​(S1−S1⊤)​(S1⊤−E0)(S1−E0)​(S1⊤−E0)=S1−S1⊤(S1−E0)​(S1⊤−E0)​(E−E0−|αS⊤|2​(S1⊤−E0)).\frac{S_{1}-E}{S_{1}-E_{0}}-|\alpha_{S^{\top}}|^{2}\frac{S_{1}-S^{\top}_{1}}{S_{1}-E_{0}}-\frac{S^{\top}_{1}-E}{S^{\top}_{1}-E_{0}}\\ =\frac{(S_{1}-E)(S^{\top}_{1}-E_{0})-|\alpha_{S^{\top}}|^{2}(S_{1}-S^{\top}_{1})(S^{\top}_{1}-E_{0})-(S^{\top}_{1}-E)(S_{1}-E_{0})}{(S_{1}-E_{0})(S^{\top}_{1}-E_{0})}\\ =\frac{-S_{1}E_{0}-ES^{\top}_{1}+S_{1}^{\top}E_{0}+S_{1}E-|\alpha_{S^{\top}}|^{2}(S_{1}-S^{\top}_{1})(S^{\top}_{1}-E_{0})}{(S_{1}-E_{0})(S^{\top}_{1}-E_{0})}\\ =\frac{S_{1}-S_{1}^{\top}}{(S_{1}-E_{0})(S^{\top}_{1}-E_{0})}\big(E-E_{0}-|\alpha_{S^{\top}}|^{2}(S_{1}^{\top}-E_{0})\big). (33)

The leading fraction is positive by assumption. Let |β|2|\beta|^{2} denote the overlap with the singlet space; since it is at least as large as the overlap with the ground state alone, it satisfies the same bound from Theorem 1. In addition, |β|2=1−|αS⊤|2|\beta|^{2}=1-|\alpha_{S^{\top}}|^{2}. Therefore,

E−E0−|αS⊤|2​(S1⊤−E0)=E−E0−(1−|β|2)​(S1⊤−E0)=E−S1⊤+|β|2​(S1⊤−E0)≥E−S1⊤+S1⊤−ES1⊤−E0​(S1⊤−E0)=0,\begin{split}E-E_{0}-|\alpha_{S^{\top}}|^{2}(S_{1}^{\top}-E_{0})&=E-E_{0}-(1-|\beta|^{2})(S_{1}^{\top}-E_{0})\\ &=E-S_{1}^{\top}+|\beta|^{2}(S_{1}^{\top}-E_{0})\\ &\geq E-S_{1}^{\top}+\frac{S_{1}^{\top}-E}{S_{1}^{\top}-E_{0}}(S_{1}^{\top}-E_{0})=0,\end{split} (34)

which confirms that the bound from Theorem 2 is tighter than that from Theorem 1.

Theorem 2 requires knowledge of the overlap |αS⊤|2|\alpha_{S^{\top}}|^{2}, which may in general be difficult to estimate. What is readily accessible is the expectation value with respect to number, zz-spin and S2S^{2} symmetries, or the corresponding penalty Hamiltonians. We now introduce a suitable penalty Hamiltonian.

Definition 1.

Let HPH_{P} be a Hermitian operator. We call it a (λ2,λP)(\lambda_{2},\lambda_{P})-singlet penalty Hamiltonian if it satisfies all of the following conditions simultaneously:

  1. 1.

    HP≥0H_{P}\geq 0,

  2. 2.

    the nullspace of HPH_{P} is the space of all singlet states,

  3. 3.

    the smallest positive eigenvalue of HPH_{P} is bounded below by λ2\lambda_{2},

  4. 4.

    the spectrum is bounded above by λP\lambda_{P}.

Such HPH_{P} can be easily constructed by an appropriate combination of penalty Hamiltonians for the number, zz-spin, and S2S^{2} symmetries. The following theorem provides a bound when |αS⊤|2|\alpha_{S^{\top}}|^{2} is unknown, but the expectation value of |ψ⟩\ket{\psi} with respect to HPH_{P} is available. This value can be approximated, e.g., with the Majorana Propagation simulator or directly with a QPU.

Theorem 3.

Let H,|E0⟩,|S1⊤⟩,|S1⟩,E0,S1⊤,S1H,\ket{E_0},\ket{S^\top_1},\ket{S_1},E_{0},S^{\top}_{1},S_{1} be as in Theorem 2. Let HPH_{P} be a (λ2,λP)(\lambda_{2},\lambda_{P})-singlet penalty Hamiltonian and let p≔⟨ψ|​HP​|ψ⟩∈[0,λ2]p\coloneqq\bra{\psi}H_{P}\ket{\psi}\in[0,\lambda_{2}]. Then

|⟨ψ|E0⟩|2≥{S1−ES1−E0−pλ2​S1−S1⊤S1−E0,S1⊤<S1,S1−ES1−E0−pλP​S1−S1⊤S1−E0,otherwise.|\innerproduct{\psi}{E_0}|^{2}\geq\begin{cases}\frac{S_{1}-E}{S_{1}-E_{0}}-\frac{p}{\lambda_{2}}\frac{S_{1}-S^{\top}_{1}}{S_{1}-E_{0}},&S^{\top}_{1}<S_{1},\\ \frac{S_{1}-E}{S_{1}-E_{0}}-\frac{p}{\lambda_{P}}\frac{S_{1}-S^{\top}_{1}}{S_{1}-E_{0}},&\rm otherwise.\end{cases} (35)
Proof.

Observe that

p=⟨ψ|​HP​|ψ⟩=(α0∗​⟨E0|+αS∗​⟨ψS|+αS⊤∗​⟨ψS⊤|)​HP​(α0​|E0⟩+αS​|ψS⟩+αS⊤​|ψS⊤⟩)=|αS⊤|2​⟨ψS⊤|​HP​|ψS⊤⟩,\begin{split}p&=\bra{\psi}H_{P}\ket{\psi}\\ &=(\alpha_{0}^{\ast}\bra{E_0}+\alpha_{S}^{\ast}\bra{\psi_S}+\alpha_{S^{\top}}^{\ast}\bra{\psi_{S^\top}})H_{P}(\alpha_{0}\ket{E_0}+\alpha_{S}\ket{\psi_S}+\alpha_{S^{\top}}\ket{\psi_{S^\top}})\\ &=|\alpha_{S^{\top}}|^{2}\bra{\psi_{S^\top}}H_{P}\ket{\psi_{S^\top}},\end{split} (36)

where we used HP​|E0⟩=HP​|ψS⟩=0H_{P}\ket{E_0}=H_{P}\ket{\psi_S}=0, since both states are singlet states. Since |ψS⊤⟩\ket{\psi_{S^\top}} is a non-singlet state, ⟨ψS⊤|​HP​|ψS⊤⟩∈[λ2,λP]\bra{\psi_{S^\top}}H_{P}\ket{\psi_{S^\top}}\in[\lambda_{2},\lambda_{P}] by definition of HPH_{P}. Therefore,

|αS⊤|2=p⟨ψS⊤|​HP​|ψS⊤⟩|\alpha_{S^{\top}}|^{2}=\frac{p}{\bra{\psi_{S^\top}}H_{P}\ket{\psi_{S^\top}}} (37)

gives

pλP≤|αS⊤|2≤pλ2.\frac{p}{\lambda_{P}}\leq|\alpha_{S^{\top}}|^{2}\leq\frac{p}{\lambda_{2}}. (38)

Since the exact value of |αS⊤|2|\alpha_{S^{\top}}|^{2} is unknown, we must account for the worst possible case. This leads to different expressions depending on whether S1⊤<S1S^{\top}_{1}<S_{1} or not. Assuming S1⊤<S1S^{\top}_{1}<S_{1} and using Theorem 2:

|⟨ψ|E0⟩|2≥S1−ES1−E0−|αS⊤|2​S1−S1⊤S1−E0≥S1−ES1−E0−pλ2​S1−S1⊤S1−E0.|\innerproduct{\psi}{E_0}|^{2}\geq\frac{S_{1}-E}{S_{1}-E_{0}}-|\alpha_{S^{\top}}|^{2}\frac{S_{1}-S^{\top}_{1}}{S_{1}-E_{0}}\geq\frac{S_{1}-E}{S_{1}-E_{0}}-\frac{p}{\lambda_{2}}\frac{S_{1}-S^{\top}_{1}}{S_{1}-E_{0}}. (39)

In the opposite case:

|⟨ψ|E0⟩|2≥S1−ES1−E0−|αS⊤|2​S1−S1⊤S1−E0≥S1−ES1−E0−pλP​S1−S1⊤S1−E0.|\innerproduct{\psi}{E_0}|^{2}\geq\frac{S_{1}-E}{S_{1}-E_{0}}-|\alpha_{S^{\top}}|^{2}\frac{S_{1}-S^{\top}_{1}}{S_{1}-E_{0}}\geq\frac{S_{1}-E}{S_{1}-E_{0}}-\frac{p}{\lambda_{P}}\frac{S_{1}-S^{\top}_{1}}{S_{1}-E_{0}}. (40)

These two cases give the required statement. ∎

Both bounds in Theorem 3 coincide at S1⊤=S1=E1S^{\top}_{1}=S_{1}=E_{1}, trivially recovering Theorem 1. We conclude with a generalization to the case where S1⊤S_{1}^{\top} is unknown.

Theorem 4.

Let H,|E0⟩,|S1⊤⟩,|S1⟩,E0,S1,HP,pH,\ket{E_0},\ket{S^\top_1},\ket{S_1},E_{0},S_{1},H_{P},p be as in Theorem 3. Then

|⟨ψ|E0⟩|2≥{S1−ES1−E0−pλ2,S1⊤<S1,S1−ES1−E0,otherwise.|\innerproduct{\psi}{E_0}|^{2}\geq\begin{cases}\frac{S_{1}-E}{S_{1}-E_{0}}-\frac{p}{\lambda_{2}},&S^{\top}_{1}<S_{1},\\ \frac{S_{1}-E}{S_{1}-E_{0}},&\rm otherwise.\end{cases} (41)
Proof.

Using Theorem 3,

|⟨ψ|E0⟩|2≥{S1−ES1−E0−pλ2​S1−S1⊤S1−E0,S1⊤<S1,S1−ES1−E0−pλP​S1−S1⊤S1−E0,otherwise.|\innerproduct{\psi}{E_0}|^{2}\geq\begin{cases}\frac{S_{1}-E}{S_{1}-E_{0}}-\frac{p}{\lambda_{2}}\frac{S_{1}-S^{\top}_{1}}{S_{1}-E_{0}},&S^{\top}_{1}<S_{1},\\ \frac{S_{1}-E}{S_{1}-E_{0}}-\frac{p}{\lambda_{P}}\frac{S_{1}-S^{\top}_{1}}{S_{1}-E_{0}},&\rm otherwise.\end{cases} (42)

For the case S1⊤<S1S_{1}^{\top}<S_{1}:

|⟨ψ|E0⟩|2≥S1−ES1−E0−pλ2​S1−S1⊤S1−E0≥S1−ES1−E0−pλ2​S1−E0S1−E0≥S1−ES1−E0−pλ2.\begin{split}|\innerproduct{\psi}{E_0}|^{2}&\geq\frac{S_{1}-E}{S_{1}-E_{0}}-\frac{p}{\lambda_{2}}\frac{S_{1}-S^{\top}_{1}}{S_{1}-E_{0}}\\ &\geq\frac{S_{1}-E}{S_{1}-E_{0}}-\frac{p}{\lambda_{2}}\frac{S_{1}-E_{0}}{S_{1}-E_{0}}\\ &\geq\frac{S_{1}-E}{S_{1}-E_{0}}-\frac{p}{\lambda_{2}}.\end{split} (43)

For the other case:

|⟨ψ|E0⟩|2≥S1−ES1−E0+pλP​S1⊤−S1S1−E0≥S1−ES1−E0.\begin{split}|\innerproduct{\psi}{E_0}|^{2}&\geq\frac{S_{1}-E}{S_{1}-E_{0}}+\frac{p}{\lambda_{P}}\frac{S_{1}^{\top}-S_{1}}{S_{1}-E_{0}}\geq\frac{S_{1}-E}{S_{1}-E_{0}}.\end{split} (44)

∎

If the relation between S1⊤S_{1}^{\top} and S1S_{1} is unknown, one can always use the weaker bound S1−ES1−E0−pλ2\frac{S_{1}-E}{S_{1}-E_{0}}-\frac{p}{\lambda_{2}}.

The lower bound computed with the Theorem above assumes the produced state is a particularly unfortunate superposition of ground and eigenstates, therefore it is expected that the real overlap is much higher that the estimated bound. We performed a separate analysis as describe below, and summarize our finding in Table 6. Our estimation of the exact overlap with the ground state was made by computing overlap between the DMRG solution and the sparse wavefunction simulation of circuit. The DMRG solution has been computed through the extraction of the determinants and related CI weights from the MPS wavefunction associated with the ground state of the actively rotated Hamiltonian. Following the same setup for the reference energies reported in Table 3, a non-spin adapted DMRG mode SymmetryType.SZ was used to solve the eigenvalue problem on the Hamiltonians for each of the two active spaces under analysis, i.e. 40 and 52 qubits. In particular, for the former we selected all the determinants with an absolute coefficient magnitude above 10−710^{-7}, and 10−610^{-6} for the latter.

Since sparse wavefunction simulator cannot effectively generate a superposition of Slater determinants constructed with active rotations, we executed DMRG on the integrals dressed with active rotations found by ADAPT-VMPE. In order to obtain the dressed integrals, h~p​q\tilde{h}_{pq} and h~p​q​r​s\tilde{h}_{pqrs}, the unitary transformation UU must be defined as

U=∏keGk​θk,U=\prod_{k}e^{G_{k}\theta_{k}}, (45)

where GkG_{k} is the generator of the kk-th orbital rotation between orbital pp and qq defined as aq†​ap−ap†​aqa_{q}^{\dagger}a_{p}-a_{p}^{\dagger}a_{q}, as in Eq. (1). Then, the unitary can be applied to the original integrals, hp​qh_{pq} and hp​q​r​sh_{pqrs}, obtaining the dressed integrals as

h~p​q=Ui​p​hi​j​Uj​r,h~p​q​r​s=Ui​p​Uj​q​hi​j​k​l​Uk​r​Ul​s,\tilde{h}_{pq}=U_{ip}{h}_{ij}U_{jr},\quad\tilde{h}_{pqrs}=U_{ip}U_{jq}{h}_{ijkl}U_{kr}U_{ls}, (46)

where hp​qh_{pq} is the original one-body tensor and hp​q​r​sh_{pqrs} is the original two-body tensor (a more detailed explanation of the procedure can be found in Reference Ratini et al. (2023)). In particular, the transformation UU is split between α\alpha and β\beta spin sectors. Following this rule, the transformation needs to be applied accordingly to the nature of the tensors, i.e. α\alpha transformation on α\alpha indexed tensors, β\beta transformation of β\beta indexed tensors.

The remaining part of the ADAPT-VMPE circuit was simulated with sparse wavefunction, truncating terms with coefficient magnitude 10−810^{-8} or less.
